zh.q: 教材只给了一张材料清单，这些东西摆成什么样的实验才说得清？
zh.concl: 教材的材料清单要摆成「一个变量一组对照」：测温度用淀粉酶加碘液，测 pH 用过氧化氢酶看气泡；回来再单独验一件事 —— 处理过的酶还能不能恢复。
points: 三个站对应教材 p.83 的分工建议：淀粉酶测温度（碘液显色）、过氧化氢酶测 pH（气泡），两站各看各的现象。
每站都有对照管，而且只有要测的那一个变量不同 —— 这就是变量控制。
读数把「颜色深不深、气泡多不多」换成一个 0–100 的数，才比得出差多少。

zh.q: 同一支酶，为什么换一个水温，碘液的颜色就不一样了？
zh.concl: 其他条件相同时，温度偏高或偏低酶活性都明显降低；最适温度在教材给的动物酶区间 35~40 ℃ 内（本课设定 37 ℃，活性记作 100 %）。
points: 两支管只有水浴温度不同：酶量、淀粉量、保温时间全都一样。
颜色来自「碘液 + 淀粉」，不是酶的颜色 —— 不显蓝说明淀粉已经被水解完了。
测温度为什么不用过氧化氢酶？教材 p.77 的 2 号管只放在 90 ℃ 水浴里、不加催化剂也冒气泡，加热本身就让 H₂O₂ 分解，气泡说不清是谁干的（由教材推出）。

zh.q: 把溶液调酸，气泡为什么几乎不冒了？
zh.concl: 其他条件相同时，pH 偏高或偏低酶活性都明显降低；最适 pH 在教材给的动物酶区间 6.5~8.0 内（本课设定 6.8）。
points: 三支管只有 pH 与「有没有酶」不同：pH 7 对照、可调 pH 实验、加蒸馏水的空白。
气泡是 H₂O₂ 分解放出的 O₂；没有酶的那支几乎不冒泡，说明气泡确实来自酶。

zh.q: 在 90 ℃ 里放过 10 分钟的酶，回到 37 ℃ 还能干活吗？
zh.concl: 温度过高会使酶的空间结构遭到破坏，使酶永久失活 —— 回到最适温度也恢复不了。
points: 回来的是同一个 37 ℃，唯一的区别是「之前被处理过」。
0.0 % 不是「测不出来」，是这支酶已经没有活性了。
读数「永久失活」、碘液的深蓝、放大窗里闭合的凹槽，是同一件事的三种写法。

zh.q: 在 0 ℃ 里冻了 10 分钟，它为什么还能醒过来？
zh.concl: 在 0 ℃ 左右时酶的活性很低，但空间结构稳定，在适宜的温度下酶的活性会升高 —— 低温不是失活，所以酶制剂适宜在低温下保存。
points: 低温改的是「反应有多快」，不是「酶还在不在」。
100.0 % 与未处理的 100.0 % 一模一样 —— 这就是「可恢复」的判据。
和第 4 步对着看：同一个读数、两种命运，区别只在处理温度。

zh.concl: 酶靠形状干活：凹槽的形状与底物相配，底物嵌进去才被切开。空间结构一破坏，凹槽没了，活性也就没了 —— 这就是「永久失活」看得见的样子。
points: 酶不是把淀粉「搬走」，是把长链切成短链。
凹槽（活性位点）的形状要与底物的形状对上，这才叫锁-钥匙。
低温时凹槽没坏，只是酶和底物都动得慢，碰上的机会就少。

zh.q: 把这支酶泡在过酸的溶液里十分钟，再调回最适 pH，它还干活吗？
zh.concl: 过酸、过碱会使酶的空间结构遭到破坏，使酶永久失活；它和温度过高是同一种后果，调回最适条件也救不回来。
points: 错误操作就在这一步：酶被泡在没调好 pH 的溶液里 → 过酸过碱 → 永久失活 → 调回 6.8 仍 0.0 %（未处理是 100.0 %）。
现象与读数一起变：气泡 0.00×、放大窗里凹槽塌陷闭合、状态读「永久失活」。
想接着做要「复位本步」或把预处理拨回「未处理」—— 那等于换一支新鲜酶。

zh.q: 考核：把这个酶的活性调到 95 % 以上
zh.concl: 考核没有新结论：温度落在教材 35–40 ℃、pH 落在教材 6.5–8.0、酶又没被处理坏，三件事同时成立才达标。
points: 只调对温度不够：pH 拖到 6.0 就掉到 93.6 %，出界。
只调对 pH 也不够：温度 30 ℃ 只有 87.8 %。
拨到 0 ℃ / 90 ℃ / 过酸 / 过碱任一处档，活性会掉到 0 或不合规，只能拨回「未处理」。

en.q: The textbook only gives a list of materials: how should they be set up so the experiment is clear?
en.concl: The textbook's materials list must be arranged as "one variable, one controlled comparison": amylase with iodine for temperature, catalase bubbles for pH; then a separate check: can a treated enzyme recover?
points: The three stations follow the division suggested on textbook p.83: amylase for temperature (iodine color), catalase for pH (bubbles), each station watching its own observation.
Each station has a control tube, and only the variable being tested differs; that is variable control.
The reading turns "how dark the color, how many bubbles" into a number from 0 to 100, so differences can be compared.

en.q: Same enzyme: why does the iodine color differ when the water temperature changes?
en.concl: With other conditions the same, enzyme activity drops clearly whether the temperature is too high or too low; the optimum lies within the textbook's 35–40 ℃ range for animal enzymes (set to 37 ℃ in this lesson, with activity recorded as 100 %).
points: The two tubes differ only in water-bath temperature: enzyme amount, starch amount and incubation time are all the same.
The color comes from "iodine + starch", not from the enzyme; no blue means the starch has been fully hydrolyzed.

Why not use catalase for temperature? Tube 2 on textbook p.77, placed only in a 90 ℃ water bath with no catalyst, also bubbles: heating alone decomposes H₂O₂, so you can't tell who made the bubbles (inferred from the textbook).

en.q: Why does bubbling nearly stop when the solution is made acidic?
en.concl: With other conditions the same, enzyme activity drops clearly whether the pH is too high or too low; the optimum lies within the textbook's 6.5–8.0 range for animal enzymes (set to 6.8 in this lesson).
points: The three tubes differ only in pH and "enzyme or not": pH 7 control, adjustable-pH test, distilled-water blank.
The bubbles are O₂ from H₂O₂ decomposition; the tube without enzyme barely bubbles, showing the bubbles really come from the enzyme.

en.q: An enzyme that spent 10 minutes at 90 ℃: can it still work back at 37 ℃?
en.concl: Excessive temperature destroys the enzyme's spatial structure and inactivates it permanently; returning to the optimum temperature can't restore it.
points: It's back at the same 37 ℃; the only difference is that it was treated before.
0.0 % isn't "unmeasurable"; this enzyme simply has no activity left.
The "permanently inactivated" reading, the dark blue iodine and the closed groove in the magnified window are three ways of writing the same thing.

en.q: Frozen at 0 ℃ for 10 minutes, why can it still wake up?
en.concl: Around 0 ℃ enzyme activity is very low but the spatial structure is stable, and activity rises again at a suitable temperature; low temperature isn't inactivation, so enzyme preparations are best stored cold.
points: Low temperature changes how fast the reaction goes, not whether the enzyme survives.
100.0 % is exactly the same as untreated 100.0 %; that's the criterion for "recoverable".
Compare with step 4: the same reading, two fates, the only difference being the treatment temperature.

en.q: What exactly does the enzyme do to the starch?
en.concl: Enzymes work by shape: the groove matches the substrate, and the substrate is cut only when it fits in. Once the spatial structure is destroyed the groove is gone, and so is the activity; that's what "permanent inactivation" looks like.
points: The enzyme doesn't "carry away" the starch; it cuts long chains into short ones.
The shape of the groove (active site) must match the shape of the substrate; that's what lock and key means.
At low temperature the groove isn't damaged; enzyme and substrate just move slowly and meet less often.

en.q: Soak this enzyme in an overly acidic solution for ten minutes, then return it to the optimum pH: does it still work?
en.concl: Too acidic or too basic conditions destroy the enzyme's spatial structure and inactivate it permanently; the consequence is the same as excessive heat, and returning to the optimum can't save it.
points: The wrong action is in this step: the enzyme is soaked in a solution whose pH wasn't adjusted → too acidic or basic → permanent inactivation → still 0.0 % back at 6.8 (untreated is 100.0 %).
Observations and readings change together: bubbles 0.00×, the groove in the magnified window collapses shut, status "permanently inactivated".
To carry on you must "reset this step" or switch the pretreatment back to "untreated", which amounts to using a fresh enzyme.

en.q: Assessment: bring this enzyme's activity above 95 %
en.concl: The assessment has no new conclusion: it passes only when the temperature is in the textbook's 35–40 ℃, the pH in the textbook's 6.5–8.0, and the enzyme hasn't been damaged by treatment, all at once.
points: Getting only the temperature right isn't enough: drag pH to 6.0 and it drops to 93.6 %, out of range.
Getting only the pH right isn't enough either: at 30 ℃ it's only 87.8 %.
Switching to any of 0 ℃ / 90 ℃ / too acidic / too basic drops activity to 0 or breaks the rules; the only fix is to switch back to "untreated".
